predecessors.note: Acceded 27 March 1948 (Princely state page); Bahawalpur (5 October 1947), Khairpur, Swat, Dir, Chitral and the Makran states joined in 1947-1948. None has a dossier yet.

capitals.name: Karachi
capitals.note: 'Karachi was its provisional national capital'; the page implies it until the 1958-1959 move.

capitals.name: Rawalpindi
capitals.note: 'de-facto national capital from 1959 to 1967 while Islamabad was under construction'.

capitals.name: Islamabad
capitals.note: Moved 'when essential development work was completed in 1966' and 'established in 1967'.

minus.text: the Khanate of Kalat, central Balochistan (about 73,000 km2; a circle of 150 km round Kalat town is the nearest the gazetteer can draw)

correction.text: the Dominion of Pakistan as at 14 August 1947: West Pakistan and East Bengal without the independent Khanate of Kalat

keyframe_review.note: 1947, 938,000 km2 (884,000 km2 by cell count): West Pakistan and East Bengal with Sylhet, as the Partition page has it ('two non-contiguous areas, East Pakistan (today Bangladesh) and West Pakistan'); the Radcliffe line 'was revealed on 17 August, two days after the partition'. The Pakistan infobox gives 881,913 km2 for the present state without East Pakistan, so the outline is credible (938,000 against about 882,000 plus 128,000). The outline lacks Kashmir (added in 1948) but includes the Khanate of Kalat, which 'remained independent until it was acceded on 27 March 1948' (Princely state page); Kalat is cut out for the 1947 year and joins in March 1948. Bahawalpur 'joined Pakistan on 5 October 1947' and stays inside. It also includes Gwadar (21 cells within 60 km), which the pages opened do not date (the Pakistan page is silent on its purchase from Oman).

1948-1962, 1.02 M km2: 299 cells (75,600 km2) are added to 1947: Gilgit-Baltistan (57,000 km2) and Azad Kashmir (10,000 km2) and the rest of the Kashmir front. The war page: 'Pakistan had control of one-third of the state' and 'By 1 November, Gilgit-Baltistan had been annexed from the Dogra dynasty'; ceasefire 'At 23.59 hrs on 1 January 1949'. The outline stands for the whole of 1948-1962 (East Pakistan included; the Raj-era Gwadar enclave included, unverified, see the 1947 note). Total 1.02 M km2 against the present infobox 881,913 km2 plus East Pakistan about 129,000: ratio 1.0.

correction.text: the 1963 outline (West Pakistan with East Pakistan and the Kashmir lands, less Shaksgam) for 1963-1971; 1972 is the keyframe below

keyframe_review.note: 1963-1972, 1.02 M km2: three cells (760 km2, 76.1-77.1 E, 35.6-36.0 N) are removed in 1963, which is the agreement signed 'on 2 March 1963': the page has Pakistan 'ceding its claim over 1,050 sq mi (2,730 km2) in Shaksgam' (Indian writers give about 5,300 km2) and gaining 750 sq mi (1,942 km2) of grazing land from China, so Cliopatria's 760 km2 under-draws the cession and draws no gain. East Pakistan stays inside the outline to the end of 1972 although Pakistan lost it on 16 December 1971 (Bangladesh Liberation War page, infobox 'Eastern territory withdrawn: 16 December 1971'): the ledger takes it in 1971 and a one-year keyframe for 1972 follows.

correction.text: West Pakistan with Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, without East Pakistan

keyframe_review.note: New one-year keyframe: Cliopatria's Pakistan outline still holds East Pakistan in 1972 and starts Bangladesh in 1973, but 'Unable to defend Dacca, the Pakistanis surrendered on 16 December 1971' and 'East Pakistan secedes from Pakistan as the People's Republic of Bangladesh'. For 1972 the 1973 outline applies.

1973-1975, 876,000 km2: the Pakistan of today less East Pakistan; infobox 'Total: 881,913 km2' (ratio 0.99). It carries Azad Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan ('The Government of Pakistan governs the western parts of the Kashmir Region, organised into separate political entities, Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan') and three cells of the Siachen glacier. The 1972 Simla Agreement turned the ceasefire line into the Line of Control (infobox 'Established: 2 July 1972').
1976-1978, 876,000 km2, the 1973 outline unchanged (one cell of difference); same page and infobox area.

1979-1982, 876,000 km2: three cells (760 km2, 65.6-71.2 E, 29.7-34.2 N) are added on the Afghan frontier and removed in 1983; no page opened dates a change on the Durand Line in these years, so the flicker is Cliopatria's noise (unverified: page budget).
1983-1986, 876,000 km2: the three Afghan-frontier cells of 1979-1982 are removed again; unverified: page budget.

1987-1995, 876,000 km2: one cell exchanged near the Siachen-Kargil sector (76.1-76.8 E, 34.6-34.9 N). The Line of Control page says the forces were 'clashing there from 1984' and gives no line change; unverified: page budget.
1996-2005, 876,000 km2: two cells added and one removed on the Chitral-Afghan frontier (71.2-71.6 E, 34.7-35.5 N), reversed in 2006; no page opened dates a change there; unverified: page budget.

2006-2023, 876,000 km2: the 1996 flicker reversed; infobox 881,913 km2 (ratio 0.99). The merger of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 2018 is internal and not on the Pakistan page.

minus.text: the Khanate of Kalat, central Balochistan (about 73,000 km2; a circle of 150 km round Kalat town is the nearest the gazetteer can draw)

region.text: West Pakistan and East Pakistan: the Muslim-majority provinces and districts, 'two non-contiguous areas'

ledger.note: 1947: Pakistan is born. 'On 14 August 1947, the new Dominion of Pakistan came into being' (Partition page); the Pakistan page gives 'Recognised dominion: 14 August 1947' and says it was 'Initially a dominion of the British Commonwealth'. Mohammad Ali Jinnah was 'sworn in as its first Governor-General in Karachi'. The Muslim-majority provinces of Punjab and Bengal were partitioned and the state had two wings.

1947: Bahawalpur joins. The Princely state page: Bahawalpur 'joined Pakistan on 5 October 1947'; the Pakistan page calls it 'the largest' of the princely states. Swat, Chitral and Dir 'joined Pakistan on independence'. [Reviewer sa-06-d, 2026-10-25: counterpart slug bahawalpur -> bahawalpur-state, the existing dossier of the same state.]

region.text: the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir

ledger.note: 1947: the war for Kashmir. 'On 22 October 1947, Pakistan's Pashtun tribal militias crossed the border of the state'; the Maharaja acceded to India on 26 October 1947; the infobox gives the war as '22 October 1947 - 1 January 1949'. Poonch rose in revolt 'at the beginning of October 1947'.

region.text: Gilgit and the Agency districts, with Hunza and Nagar whose rulers had written to Jinnah

ledger.note: 1947: Gilgit comes to Pakistan. 'By 1 November, Gilgit-Baltistan had been annexed from the Dogra dynasty' (war page); the Gilgit Scouts took the Dogra governor into custody on 1 November and raised the Pakistan flag on 2 November (Gilgit Agency page).

region.text: Mirpur, Muzaffarabad and Poonch: the part of the princely state Pakistan held at the ceasefire

ledger.note: 1947: Mirpur and the western Kashmir districts. 'Mirpur was captured by the tribal forces on 25 November 1947'; Muzaffarabad was entered on 22 October. The page gives no date for the proclamation of Azad Kashmir; the region is the present Azad Kashmir.

region.text: the Khanate of Kalat, central Balochistan (about 73,000 km2; a circle of 150 km round Kalat town is the nearest the gazetteer can draw)

ledger.note: 1948: Kalat accedes. 'The state remained independent until it was acceded on 27 March 1948.' The page gives no extent; the region is a 150 km circle round Kalat for a state of about 73,000 km2, which includes the Makran-facing south only in part. [Reviewer sa-06-d, 2026-10-25: counterpart slug kalat -> khanate-of-kalat, the existing dossier of the same state.]

1948: Skardu and Baltistan. 'The Pakistani attacked the Skardu on 10 February 1948' and 'On 14 August, Thapa had to surrender Skardu to the Pakistani Army'; the page does not give the year of the surrender in that sentence, so August 1948 follows from the February siege.

region.text: the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, divided along the ceasefire line

ledger.note: 1949: the ceasefire. 'At 23.59 hrs on 1 January 1949, a United Nations-mediated ceasefire came into effect'; 'India and Pakistan signed the Karachi Agreement in July 1949' and Pakistan held 'one-third of the state'. The line became the Line of Control in 1972.

1956: the Dominion becomes the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. 'Pakistan adopted a republican constitution in 1956 and became an Islamic republic' (infobox 'Republic: 23 March 1956'); the colour and dossier continue.

1958-1959: the capital leaves Karachi. 'In 1958, a commission was constituted to select a suitable site near Rawalpindi for the national capital'; Rawalpindi 'served as the de-facto national capital from 1959 to 1967 while Islamabad was under construction'; Islamabad followed in 1966-1967.

region.text: the Shaksgam strip on the Karakoram watershed (Cliopatria's 1963 loss, 3 cells, 760 km2)

ledger.note: 1963: the border agreement with China. Signed 'on 2 March 1963': Pakistan ceded its claim over about 2,730 km2 in the Shaksgam, China 'relinquished its claims over Hunza', and Article 6 provides that 'pending the final settlement of the Kashmir dispute between India and Pakistan, a fresh treaty will be drawn up'. India says the agreement 'is invalid'.

1971: the Bangladesh Liberation War. The army 'launched Operation Searchlight against East Pakistanis on the night of 25 March 1971'; '26 March 1971 is considered the official Independence Day of Bangladesh'; a provisional government was formed on 17 April 1971 in Meherpur District.

1971: the surrender at Dhaka. 'India joined the war on 3 December 1971 in support of the Mukti Bahini' after a Pakistani strike on Indian air bases the same day; 'Unable to defend Dacca, the Pakistanis surrendered on 16 December 1971.'

1971: East Pakistan becomes Bangladesh. 'East Pakistan secedes from Pakistan as the People's Republic of Bangladesh' (infobox result); the Pakistan page has 'Eastern territory withdrawn: 16 December 1971'. Cliopatria keeps East Pakistan in the Pakistan outline to 1972 and starts Bangladesh in 1973.

wars.name: Indo-Pakistani War of 1947-1948

zones.text: the princely state, divided by the ceasefire line of 1 January 1949

wars.outcome: A United Nations ceasefire at 23.59 hrs on 1 January 1949 left Pakistan 'control of one-third of the state' (Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan) and India two-thirds; the Karachi Agreement of July 1949 fixed the line.
wars.note: Poonch rose in October 1947; Mirpur fell on 25 November 1947; Skardu was attacked on 10 February 1948 and surrendered on 14 August (year not on the sentence).

wars.name: Indo-Pakistani War of 1965
wars.outcome: The Pakistan page says only 'the second war with India in 1965, resulting in an economic downturn and widespread public discontent in 1967'; no border moved in Cliopatria.
wars.note: A gap-filler may open the 1965 war page for the Rann of Kutch and Chhamb exchanges; page silent.

wars.name: Bangladesh Liberation War
wars.outcome: 'Bangladeshi-Indian victory': Pakistani forces surrendered at Dhaka on 16 December 1971 and East Pakistan became Bangladesh.
wars.note: 26 March - 16 December 1971; India entered on 3 December.

wars.name: Siachen conflict
wars.outcome: The Line of Control page says only that the forces have been 'clashing there from 1984'; the line is not drawn north of its last point and no outcome is given.
wars.note: Cliopatria's Pakistan outline holds three of the glacier's seven cells and India's none.

wars.name: Kargil War
wars.outcome: 'Military tension between the two countries in the Kargil district led to the Kargil War of 1999' (Pakistan page); no change of the Line of Control is recorded on either page.
wars.note: Page silent on dates and result.

certainty.note: The Radcliffe line 'was revealed on 17 August' 1947 and bounds both wings; the Kashmir front is soft until the ceasefire of 1 January 1949.

The Durand Line (1893, inherited in 1947), the Radcliffe line, the 1963 Chinese boundary and the Line of Control from 1949 (relaid 1972, 740-776 km) are fixed lines; the Siachen sector is not delimited and is soft.

notes: Written by sa-06-d from nine pages (budget up to 5: Islamabad is an extra page for the capitals; Partition, Princely state and Gilgit Agency were opened for british-raj). CLIOPATRIA ROW: shapes 1947-2024 are consistent with the pages except (1) the 1947 outline includes the Khanate of Kalat, independent until 27 March 1948, and the Gwadar enclave of Oman (the pages are silent on Gwadar's 1958 purchase; a gap-filler should open the Gwadar page; the ledger has no Gwadar event); (2) East Pakistan stays in the outline for 1972 (new one-year keyframe 1972); (3) the 1963 Shaksgam cession is drawn as 760 km2 against the page's 2,730 km2 (or 5,300 km2 by Indian writers) and China's 1,942 km2 grant to Pakistan is not drawn; (4) Siachen is split three cells to Pakistan and none to India; (5) the 1979-1982, 1987 and 1996-2005 flickers on the Afghan and Kashmir frontiers are unexplained noise. NOT RESOLVED: the accession dates of Khairpur, Swat, Dir, Chitral, Amb, Las Bela, Makran and Kharan (Princely state page: 'on independence' or silent); Junagadh's 1947 accession to Pakistan and annexation by India (not on the pages); the Sylhet referendum, the NWFP referendum and the Balochistan decision of 1947 (Partition page silent); the One Unit scheme 1955-1970; the 1971 western-front changes (Chhamb, Turtuk) and the 1965 war's exchanges; the Kargil war's dates; Siachen's 1984 start (LoC page: 'clashing there from 1984'); the FATA merger of 2018. COUNTERPARTS WITHOUT A DOSSIER: kalat (Khanate of Kalat, to 27 March 1948), bahawalpur (to 5 October 1947), and the princely states of the north-west (Swat, Dir, Chitral, Amb, Khairpur, Las Bela, Makran, Kharan). people-s-republic-of-bangladesh and republic-of-india are other sa-06 batches. RULERS: none; the Pakistan page names Jinnah as first Governor-General and no list. Gazetteer names: Kalat is drawn as a 150 km circle round 66.6 E, 28.9 N; 'Kalat' as a place is in the gazetteer only as Qalat, Afghanistan.
